text: Lesson 17 explained what CSPM does in general: continuous scanning for configuration risk. This lesson gets specific -- the actual settings that show up, over and over, in real CSPM findings lists across both Azure and AWS. None of these are exotic. They're ordinary settings that someone left wrong, which is exactly why a continuous scanner catches so many of them.

The first pattern is a storage resource -- an S3 bucket or an Azure Storage account -- accidentally left open to public read access, exposing whatever's inside to anyone with the URL. The second is an overly permissive security group: a rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0, meaning the entire internet, on a sensitive port like 22 for SSH. The third is an IAM policy or role granting far more access than the job actually requires -- broad, wildcard permissions handed out because it was easier than scoping them down.

Written out, these look almost too simple to matter: a security group rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22, a storage account with public access enabled, an IAM policy whose Action and Resource fields are both just a wildcard, asterisk. That's the point -- a CSPM tool doesn't need to be clever to catch any of these. It just needs to check every resource, every time, against the baseline that says none of those three should look like that.

Two more checks round out the list. Encryption at rest can be disabled, or set to a weaker configuration than the organization's baseline requires, on a resource that should always be encrypted. And multi-factor authentication can simply not be enforced on a privileged or admin account, leaving it reachable with a password alone -- a gap CSPM tools flag because privileged accounts are exactly where an attacker wants to land first.

Public storage, an open security group, excessive IAM permissions, missing encryption, unenforced MFA -- five ordinary settings, and five of the most common findings a CSPM scan produces. Next, Lesson 19 looks at the real tools that run these checks at cloud scale: Microsoft Defender for Cloud and AWS Security Hub.
